item.title: Tsutenkaku Tower: The Heart of Retro Shinsekai — Guide
item.description: Tsutenkaku is the symbol of old, down-to-earth Osaka. The current tower dates from 1956, a rebuild of a 1912 original that mimicked the Eiffel Tower, and it rises above Shinsekai, a district frozen in a cheerfully retro version of the early twentieth century. Its observation decks give views across the south of the city, and enshrined near the top is Billiken, an American-born good-luck figure whose feet visitors rub for fortune.

item.title: Kushikatsu Guide: Osaka's Deep-Fried Skewers & the No-Double-Dip Rule
item.description: Kushikatsu — skewers of meat, seafood, and vegetables, breaded, deep-fried to a golden crunch, and dunked in a tangy communal sauce — is one of Osaka’s great comfort foods and the pride of the retro Shinsekai district. Cheap, crispy, endlessly varied, and washed down with cold beer, it’s working-class Osaka eating at its most fun. It also comes with the city’s single most famous food rule: no double-dipping. This guide explains what kushikatsu is, the all-important sauce etiquette, what to order, and where to eat it.

item.title: Shinsekai & Tsutenkaku Guide: Osaka's Retro Heart
item.description: Step into Shinsekai (“New World”) and you step back into a Showa-era Osaka of glowing retro signs, kushikatsu smoke, and cheerful chaos. Built in 1912 around the Tsutenkaku tower — modelled half on Paris’s Eiffel Tower and half on Coney Island — this once-futuristic district fell on hard times and reinvented itself as the city’s most nostalgic, down-to-earth, photogenic neighbourhood. It’s the spiritual home of kushikatsu (deep-fried skewers), presided over by Billiken, the funny-faced god of “things as they ought to be.

item.title: Spa World Osaka Guide: The Giant Themed Bath Complex
item.description: Beside the retro neon of Shinsekai looms Spa World — a vast, slightly surreal multi-floor bathing complex where you can soak in a Roman bath, a Finnish sauna, an Islamic-tiled pool, a Balinese spa, and a Japanese rotenburo, all under one roof. Part onsen, part water park, part kitsch theme attraction, it’s one of Osaka’s most fun and affordable ways to relax — a place to spend hours bathing, sweating, swimming, and recovering from a day of takoyaki and walking.

item.title: Osaka Sightseeing: Top 20 Spots from Dotonbori to the Castle & Beyond
item.description: Osaka is Japan’s third-largest city and its most underrated — a place where the quality of the sightseeing is consistently higher than the tourist maps suggest. Beyond the Dotonbori canal and Osaka Castle, the city contains one of Japan’s oldest shrines (Sumiyoshi Taisha, predating Buddhism’s arrival in Japan), a genuinely remarkable retro district in Shinsekai, and a mid-century coffee shop neighbourhood in Nakazakicho that feels nothing like the Japan in guidebooks.

item.title: Osaka Street Food Guide: Dotonbori & Shinsekai Best Eats
item.description: Osaka Street Food Guide: Dotonbori, Shinsekai & the Best Eats in Japan’s Kitchen There is a word in Osaka that tells you everything you need to know about this city’s relationship with food: kuidaore (食い倒れ), which translates roughly to “eat until you drop.” No other city in Japan wears its appetite so proudly. If you’re searching for a comprehensive Osaka street food guide covering Dotonbori, Shinsekai, and the best eats across the city, you’ve come to the right place — because after fifteen years of living in Japan and making countless trips to Osaka with an empty stomach and a full sense of adventure, I can tell you with absolute certainty: this is the greatest street food city in Asia.
